# Thermal Response of a Lithium Vapor Divertor to Cyclical Operation

Matthew S. Parsons1 · Margaret Porcelli2 · Eric D. Emdee1 · Robert J. Goldston1,2

Accepted: 23 January 2025 / Published online: 14 February 2025 © The Author(s) 2025

Abstract The lithium vapor divertor concept is being developed as a method to achieve detached divertor conditions in a tokamak while minimizing impurity radiation losses from the core plasma. SOLPS-ITER modeling has previously been used to identify some of the geometric constraints and required lithium evaporation rate of a lithium vapor divertor in a mediumsized tokamak during steady-state operation. Here an updated conceptual design based on these operating requirements is introduced and the thermal response of the system is modeled during cyclical operation, consistent with operation in a shortpulse tokamak. Controllability of the temperature of the lithium capillary porous system (CPS) is achieved by adopting a design where there is no line-of-sight for radiation from the plasma to reach the heated CPS surface. Operational strategies to minimize the amount of lithium evaporated between plasma discharges while achieving steady evaporation rates during plasma discharges are discussed and modeled here. The optimal feedforward control strategy demonstrated in this work is to ramp up the temperature of the evaporator as quickly as possible immediately before a plasma discharge and then reduce the heating to match the desired steady-state net evaporation rate just before the plasma discharge begins, allowing the thermal inertia of the system to stabilize the evaporation rate during the first second of the plasma discharge.

Keywords  Lithium Vapor Divertor · Divertor Detachment ·  Pulsed Tokamak

## Introduction

In a tokamak fusion reactor, an enormous amount of power will be directed toward the divertor where the heat flux must be spread out over a large enough area to prevent damage to the divertor components. To accomplish this, a common approach is to radiatively cool the plasma enough to reduce the peak heat flux at the divertor target to below about 10 MW/m2 . This radiative cooling has usually been achieved by introducing gases such as nitrogen, neon, and argon into the boundary plasma. A primary concern with introducing these impurity gases is that a relatively small concentration of them inside the core of a fusion plasma can make burning plasma conditions unreachable [1]. Since the impurity tolerance of the core plasma increases as the atomic number decreases, and noting that the cooling power of helium is too weak to be useful for mitigating the divertor heat fluxes, the

lowest-Z impurity that could be introduced to radiatively cool the plasma is lithium. The lithium vapor divertor concept is being developed to provide the basis for radiatively cooling the divertor plasma of a tokamak with lithium [2]. The original concept involved a series of connected chambers containing lithium vapor maintained at different temperatures to provide a large volume for cooling the divertor plasma while effectively trapping lithium within the divertor. The dynamics of the lithium vapor in such a system have been both modeled and tested in small-scale laboratory experiments [3–6]. This early work led to a geometrical simplification to eliminate the series of connected boxes in favor of a single box, which was predicted to achieve the desired heat flux mitigation while releasing only a small amount of lithium impurities out of the divertor region [7]. Additional modeling work has helped to refine the vapor divertor concept, including optimization of the lithium evaporation rate, the location where lithium is introduced into the system, and strategies for gas fueling of the plasma to minimize the amount of lithium that escapes the divertor [8–11]. This previous SOLPS-ITER modeling work on the lithium vapor divertor has focused on assessing divertor

The work described here will apply constraints based on those SOLPS-ITER results to develop further insight into how a lithium evaporator could be implemented in NSTX-U during a possible future campaign focused on liquid lithium plasma-facing component development [12]. The operation and design of a lithium evaporator for a short-pulse tokamak is necessarily different from the operation and design of such an evaporator for a long-pulse or steady-state tokamak. In any typical operating scenario the radiation from the divertor plasma should provide more than enough power to maintain a sufficient evaporative flux of lithium. In a steady-state scenario the excess heat will have to be removed, which means that heat pipes will likely need to be integrated into the lithium evaporator. However, in a short-pulse tokamak it may be suitable to allow the evaporator system to cool down on its own between plasma discharges without the use of heat pipes. In a steady-state scenario it may also be appropriate to allow the divertor radiation to heat the lithium evaporator up to its operating point slowly over many seconds as the plasma is ramped-up, while in a short-pulse tokamak the evaporator will need to be able to reach its operating point within about a second of when the plasma discharge begins. Toward developing the engineering basis for a lithium vapor divertor, the work presented in this paper demonstrates a preliminary effort to understand the thermal response of a lithium vapor divertor given the transient cycling it would undergo in a short-pulse tokamak experiment. In Section “Operational Target and Key Constraints”, the key design criteria relevant to the thermal cycling are discussed. In Section “Design for Temperature Controllability” a design for the geometry of the vapor divertor is introduced to allow the temperature to be controlled during transient loading of the system by radiation from the divertor plasma. In Section “Temperature Ramp-up Before Discharges” a reduced model of the divertor module’s embedded heating system is presented and used to quantify the trade-off between the temperature ramp-rate of the system and the amount of lithium used up before discharges. In Section “Evaporation Rate Control During Plasma Discharges” the heater model is applied to identify the optimal heating strategy to maintain a constant lithium evaporation rate during plasma discharges given the thermal inertia of the system. Finally, in Section “Evaporative Cooling and Repeated Cycling” the importance of the evaporative cooling and lithium recycling are discussed, along with a tally of how much lithium is used up during each phase of operation with repeated cycling of the system. While the work here is focused on a combination of parameters specific to NSTX-U, the results are qualitatively applicable to other tokamaks of a similar size or pulse duration, and the approach can be easily

adapted to perform preliminary parameter scoping tests for other tokamaks as well.

## Operational Target and Key Constraints

The key operating parameter for a lithium vapor divertor is the gross evaporation rate of lithium from the evaporator surface. For a medium-sized tokamak with 10 MW of heating power, SOLPS-ITER modeling of a previous vapor divertor design predicts that a gross evaporation rate on the order of 1023 s −1 can mitigate a peak parallel heat flux of 100 MW/m2 down to below 10 MW/m2 at the strike point [9]. Therefore, for this design activity 1023 s −1 is used as the target gross evaporation rate for the lithium evaporator system. As imagined here, the evaporator system would be made up of 12 identical modules sitting in the private flux region of the divertor, each resembling something like a box with an opening directed toward the strike point, placed toroidally around the machine to produce a highly symmetric source of lithium vapor at the divertor surface. Interaction between the lithium vapor and the plasma in the outer divertor produces radiation that dissipates the plasma heat fluxes to the divertor target surface. Previous SOLPS-ITER modeling has identified this setup as optimal for achieving the required heat flux mitigation while minimizing the amount of lithium that reaches the core, where it dilutes the fuel and in higher concentrations higher than a few percent can prevent access to burning plasma conditions [10, 11]. A poloidal crosssection of this system is depicted schematically in Fig. 1. The essential features of the module include a capillary porous system (CPS) for wicking lithium to the surface of the evaporator, and heaters embedded in the module to control the temperature of the lithium in the evaporator and so the evaporation rate. To develop a design that is consistent with the geometry of a medium-sized spherical tokamak, we will take the evaporator system to be located inside a major radius of 45 cm. Given this, the horizontal length of a single evaporator module must be less than about 23 cm. To provide some margin for the enclosure around the evaporator surface, the length of the lithium-covered surface is taken here to be 20 cm. Ongoing plasma modeling work suggests that an evaporator system with an opening of about 4 cm performs better than a system with a height of either 2 cm or 8 cm. Accordingly, a height of 5 cm is chosen for the present study so that the total surface area of a single evaporator is an even 100 cm2. Evaporation is a surface phenomenon, so the evaporation rate of lithium is the product of the surface area and the evaporation rate per unit area, which itself is determined by the surface temperature. Taking an analytical expression for the evaporation rate per unit surface area [13] as a function of the surface temperature, in combination with

At this temperature, it is expected that refractory metals are the only materials that can tolerate the highly corrosive nature of molten lithium [14]. Tungsten may be the most reactor-relevant option, given its higher melting temperature, thermal conductivity, strength, and significantly lower neutron activation than the other refractory metals. However, given tungsten’s high cost and difficulty to machine, molybdenum is taken to be the material of choice for initial prototyping of an evaporator module.

## Design for Temperature Controllability

As discussed above, the key operating parameter to control in the lithium vapor divertor is the gross lithium evaporation rate, which is a highly nonlinear function of the lithium surface temperature. Note that the gross evaporation rate must be distinguished from the net evaporation rate, which depends on the partial pressure of lithium vapor at the surface of the evaporator. The net evaporation therefore depends on the amount of lithium that builds up in the divertor as a result of plasma recycling, and this will be discussed further in Section “Evaporative Cooling and Repeated Cycling”. In order to maintain a specific surface temperature, and in turn evaporation rate, it is necessary to balance all of the inputs and outputs of power within the system during operation

of the plasma. According to SOLPS-ITER modeling of the targeted plasma scenario, the power deposited on the evaporator system by radiation emitted from the plasma is at least an order of magnitude higher than the power required to sustain the lithium evaporation during plasma operation. In a steady-state power plant scenario the evaporator system would be designed with active cooling to remove heat at the specific rate required for the reactor’s operational design point, and could be allowed to heat up from the plasma radiation throughout the slow plasma ramp-up period of a large tokamak reactor. However, for a short-pulse tokamak the challenge is more complex: to design the system with sufficient operational flexibly to be used with a wide range of plasma operating scenarios, and to be turned on and off and reach the desired operating point within a few seconds. The approach chosen in this work to mitigate the challenge of heating due to plasma radiation in a short-pulse tokamak is to design the vapor divertor with a geometry such that there is no direct line-of-sight from the divertor plasma to the lithium-coated CPS where the evaporation rate is controlled. By geometrically isolating the upper part of the system where the plasma radiation is deposited from the lower part of the system where the lithium vapor source is located, the resulting thermal decoupling of these regions allows the lithium vapor source to be controlled without the need for active cooling. One version of such an evaporator module is depicted in Fig. 1. If the lithium CPS is not being heated directly by the plasma radiation, then the impact of the radiative heating on the CPS is limited by the finite thermal diffusivity

Taking the diffusion time 휏 to be related to the distance L and diffusivity D as 휏= L2∕2D , there should be a delay of roughly 20 s between when the plasma begins depositing heat and when the lithium CPS is impacted by it. During a 5-s plasma discharge, this effectively removes the plasma radiation as a factor from the power balance of the lithium CPS. The caveat to this design choice is that the lithium vapor itself cannot reach the divertor plasma by traveling in a straight line, and therefore the angled reflector surface of the box must be hot enough that lithium vapor effectively bounces (i.e. deposits and reevaporates) off of it quickly enough to supply the plasma at the required rate. More detailed assessment of this will be addressed in future work. The thermal decoupling between the upper and lower sections of the module, needed to achieve control of the lithium CPS surface temperature, can be quantified better through simulation of the system. Here, 3D simulations of the heat diffusion problem for one evaporator module have been performed using MATLAB based on the geometry shown in Fig. 1. In this model, the walls have a thickness of 2 mm, the toroidal length of the system is 20 cm (into the page), the lower section has a height and width of 5 cm, and the upper section has a height of 5 cm and width of 10 cm. For simplicity, and to provide a conservative estimate of the rate of power transfer, the entire module is treated as being made of molybdenum, with mass density 10.28 g/cm3 , heat capacity 0.25 J/g/K, and thermal conductivity 0.138 W/mm/K. The boundary conditions are that all surfaces experience radiative cooling with an emissivity of 0.1, consistent with polished molybdenum, except for the surface of the lithium CPS that is given an emissivity of 0.05 consistent with previous experimental findings [15]. The lithium surface also experiences evaporative cooling based on an analytical model of the temperature-dependent lithium evaporation rate [13] with a heat of vaporization of 150 kJ/mol. An input heating power of 0.3 MW/m2 is added to the ceiling and floor of the module, as well as the under side of the angled portion of the module as a conservative estimate of the power deposited by plasma radiation based on results from SOLPS-ITER modeling for a high-powered NSTX-U scenario. A limitation of the SOLPS-ITER modeling is that it does not include thermal radiation of the lithium vapor inside the divertor module. However, given the lithium vapor temperature of about 1200 K calculated by SOLPS-ITER, with a maximum emissivity of 0.05 for solid lithium, the heat flux deposited on the inside of the module from the thermal radiation from the lithium vapor should be no more than about 0.006 MW/m2 . The heat flux required to sustain the target evaporation rate is at least 0.2 MW/m2 , so the

thermal radiation of the lithium vapor is not expected to be significant in the overall power balance of the system. The results of this modeling are shown in Fig. 2. While the temperatures of the molybdenum surfaces in the upper part of the evaporator module increase exponentially throughout the period of the plasma discharge (gray shaded period) due to the deposited plasma radiation, there is a clear delay in the temperature response of the lithium CPS. The surface temperature of the lithium CPS is found not to change by more than a degree within the 5-s period of the plasma discharge. This delay is consistent with the ∼20 s diffusion time estimated above, and the peak in the temperature rise actually occurs several minutes after the discharge completes. Rerunning the model confirms that even if the conservative 0.3 MW/m2 incident heat flux is doubled to 0.6 MW/m2 , it has no impact on the time-delay. This guarantees that control of the lithium CPS temperature, and in turn control of the primary lithium evaporation rate, can be achieved without consideration for the power deposited by the plasma radiation. It must be noted that 10 min after the discharge the lithium CPS is now much hotter that it was originally, which begs the question of whether the temperature would ratchet up over time and prevent consistent operation. To address this question, it is necessary to consider a more complete scenario where the lithium CPS is actively heated to reach the target evaporation rate of about 1023 s −1 . Since the heat lost through evaporation is the largest power loss mechanism in the system, it is essential to account for this. An example of this more realistic operation of the full evaporator system over five cycles of plasma discharges,

## Temperature Ramp‑up Before Discharges

The previous section shows that the upper and lower sections of the evaporator module are effectively thermally decoupled, such that the radiation from the plasma does not impact the temperature of the lithium CPS. Given this, it is reasonable to proceed with modeling the temperature response of the lithium CPS without including the heating due to plasma radiation of the upper part of the module. Accordingly, it is be assumed that conductive heat transfer between the bottom surface of the system and the rest of the system are

negligible and therefore the bottom part of the system can be modeled as just the horizontally flat piece as depicted in Fig. 4. This simplification also makes it easier to include the appropriate material parameters for each layer. The lithium CPS is modeled as a 5 mm layer of pure lithium with mass density 0.534 g/cm3 , heat capacity 3.57 J/g/K, and thermal conductivity 0.085 W/mm/K. The bottom of the enclosure is modeled as a 2 mm layer of molybdenum. The heater is modeled as a sandwich of 1 mm layers of alumina with a 0.5 mm layer of FeCrAl between them. The alumina is taken to have a mass density 3.80 g/cm3 , heat capacity 0.88 J/g/K, and thermal conductivity 0.025 W/mm/K, and the FeCrAl is taken to have a mass density 7.15 g/cm3 , heat capacity 0.70 J/g/K, and thermal conductivity 0.020 W/mm/K. Below the heater an additional 1 mm molybdenum layer is added, both to protect the alumina layer from any possible contact with stray lithium and as a heat shield with low emissivity. Each layer has areal dimensions of 50 mm by 200 mm. In practice the molybdenum heat shield would fully surround the alumina and FeCrAl layers, so a surface emissivity of 0.1 is applied everywhere except the top of the lithium CPS. The top of the lithium CPS has the same boundary condition of thermal radiation with an emissivity of 0.05 plus evaporative cooling as described above for the previous model. Volumetric heat generation is applied uniformly within the FeCrAl layer to represent resistive heating. This model is used in the remainder of this paper. It is desirable to keep the lithium CPS above the melting point of lithium, about 180 C, between discharges to improve the responsiveness of the system by avoiding the

To achieve this, a “pre-heating” of the system should be applied at the beginning of the day, and applied as needed between plasma discharges to ensure that the lithium does not resolidify. While the lithium wetting should improve with increasing temperature, the evaporation rate will also increase with the temperature and result in wasted lithium. The temperature should therefore be maintained low enough to prevent significant evaporation of lithium in between plasma discharges. As a target value, we limit the amount of lithium used up during pre-heating to the equivalent of one plasma discharge, being 5 s of operation at an evaporation rate of 1023 s −1 totaling 5.78 g of lithium per discharge. Assuming that the pre-heating is applied throughout the entire day, this amount of lithium evaporation could be averaged over an 8-h day of operation, equating to a limit of 1.7 × 1019 s −1 of lithium evaporation during pre-heating. The steady-state evaporation rate of the system for different amounts of pre-heating power per module is calculated using the layered model described above, and the results are shown in Fig. 5. The pre-heating powers shown here all satisfy the criteria that the temperature must be above the melting point of lithium, but low enough that the evaporation rate will remain below 1.7 × 1019 s −1 . Note that the evaporation rate is a highly nonlinear function of the temperature, with the evaporation rate depicted on a logarithmic scale here. After pre-heating the system to melt the lithium and achieve suitable lithium wetting of the CPS, a temperature ramp-up is necessary immediately preceding each discharge so that the system is producing the desired flux of lithium vapor throughout the entire duration of the plasma discharge. The heat of vaporization of lithium is about 150 kJ/mol, so the minimum heating power applied to the system to maintain an evaporation rate of 1023 s −1 is about 24 kW, or

about 2 kW per module. Accounting for radiative losses, the minimum is numerically found to be closer to 4.3 kW per module given the “sandwich” model as described above. In principle, performing the ramp-up at the highest heating power possible will minimize the amount of lithium that is wasted before the plasma discharge. While there do not appear to be commercially available heaters suitable for this specific application, preliminary scoping work suggests that a heater similar in construction to the sandwich of alumina and FeCrAl described above may be able to produce 10 kW of resistive heating power within prescribed safety limits for prototype testing. Accordingly, 10 kW is taken to be the maximum heating power for a single divertor module considered in this work. Additional work will be needed to ensure that the design of the heater and support structures is compatible with the magnetic field of a tokamak, though that is beyond the scope of this activity. To assess the amount of lithium used up during the rampup phase, the thermal model is deployed to identify the amount of time required to ramp-up the temperature of the lithium CPS to achieve an evaporation rate of 1023 s −1 for the full divertor system. For these simulations, the system is first pre-heated to reach steady-state at a power of 30 W and then the power is turned up to a fixed value between 5 kW and 10 kW until the target evaporation rate is achieved. The time domain of the simulation is iteratively fine-tuned to identify the required ramp-up time to the nearest 0.1 s. The results are shown in Fig. 6. As expected, a shorter ramp-up time is needed for higher heating powers, and accordingly less lithium is used up in the process. At a heating power of 10 kW, less than 4 g of lithium would be used during the rampup period before each plasma discharge. ## Evaporation Rate Control During Plasma Discharges

In order to make meaningful inferences from pulsed plasma experiments with a lithium vapor divertor, it is important that the lithium evaporation rate be maintained at a relatively constant level throughout the period of the plasma discharge. Feedback control of the evaporation rate would likely depend on thermocouple measurements, which are limited in utility given their relative uncertainty on the order of several percent and their response time on the order of a second. Since the evaporation rate is a highly nonlinear function of the temperature and the plasma discharge is only several seconds long, feedback control based on thermocouple measurements would be quite challenging. Given this, feedforward control of the heaters is assessed here as an option to maintain a constant lithium evaporation rate during the period of the plasma discharge. The primary challenge for feedforward control of the evaporator system is the thermal response time of the system due to its finite thermal diffusivity. To understand how quickly the heat can move through different layers of the system, the thermal diffusion time can again be approximated as 휏= L2∕2D , now with the material-dependent diffusivities and layer thicknesses. The diffusion time through each layer should be approximately as follows: 0.03 s for the FeCrAl heating element, 0.07 s for the alumina electrical insulation layer, 0.04 s for the molybdenum enclosure, and 0.28 s for the lithium layer. The large diffusion time for the lithium

layer is driven primarily by its thickness. Since the lithium layer is the rate-limiting step in the system response, there is a significant advantage to reducing the thickness of this layer if possible. Generally speaking, reducing the thermal mass of the system will improve its time response. The faster the system is ramped up, the larger the temperature gradient across the system is and therefore the further away the system is from thermodynamic equilibrium when it reaches the target evaporation rate. This means that after the ramp-up is complete, the evaporation rate will overshoot the target as excess heat is transferred from the hot heater to the cooler lithium surface. This can be observed in Fig. 7 where the system is ramped up at various heating rates to the point where the target evaporation rate is achieved ( t = 0 ), and then the heating power is held constant at 4.3 kW for a 5-second period. In all cases, there is an overshoot of the target evaporation rate and the evaporation peaks just over 1 s into the discharge phase. However, the 5 kW ramp-up power allows for the evaporation rate to remain within about 1% of the target rate throughout the plasma discharge period, while the 10 kW ramp-up power leads to an overshoot of the target rate of about 9% and fails to stabilize within the 5-second discharge period. The trade-off in the choice of the ramp-up power is the amount of lithium used up in the rampup phase, as discussed in the previous section and depicted in Fig. 6. Assuming that there are restrictions on the amount of lithium that can be evaporated into the tokamak during a single experimental campaign, it is advantageous to use the highest ramp-up power available to minimize the amount of

## Evaporative Cooling and Repeated Cycling

Evaporative cooling is a key power loss mechanism for the system, and therefore the system operation is highly sensitive to changes in the evaporation rate. SOLPS-ITER modeling shows that the plasma can redeposit up to 90% of the lithium vapor inside the module [11], building up a high partial pressure of lithium vapor and dramatically changing the net evaporation rate of lithium during the plasma discharge phase. The SOLPS-ITER modeling further shows that the lithium atoms returning from the plasma have a temperature of about 1600 K, and the temperature of the lithium vapor cloud in the divertor is nominally a particle flux-weighted

average between the temperature of the evaporating atoms and the temperature of the recycling atoms. To account for the difference in kinetic energy between the evaporating and condensing atoms, an extra 3/2 R(Tvapor −Tsurface) is deposited onto the evaporator surface with the recycling lithium particles. If the lithium recycling rate can be taken to be roughly constant throughout the plasma discharge period, then the feedforward heating strategy described above can still be used with adjustments needed to the timing and heating power. Specifically, with respect to the zero recycling scenario, the hand-off between the fast ramp-up and the constant heating power during the plasma phase needs to be shifted to an earlier time to allow for a larger overshoot of the evaporation rate after the fast ramp-up, and the heating power during the discharge needs to be reduced significantly to match the reduction in the net evaporation rate (e.g. down to 500 W with 90% lithium recycling). Given the reduction in heating power needed to achieve a given gross evaporation rate when the lithium recycling increases, the operational space of the evaporator system increases with the lithium recycling rate. This can be seen in Fig. 9, which shows the steady-state gross evaporation rate as a function of the heating power in the case when there is no lithium recycling and the case when there is 90% lithium recycling into the module. At 10 kW of heating power per module the steady-state gross evaporation rate of the full divertor system is 2.4 × 1023 s −1 when there is no lithium recycling, but this increases by an order of magnitude to 2.9 × 1024 s −1 if the lithium recycling rate is 90%. While the lithium recycling may improve the experimental flexibility of the system for a given heater design, it cannot replace the need for high-powered heaters to quickly ramp-up the

In the absence of an active cooling system, the evaporative cooling also drives how quickly the lithium evaporation can be curtailed after a plasma discharge is completed. To examine this, a simulation of multiple cycles of operation is shown in Fig. 10. Here, the system is repeatedly cycled with 10 kW of ramp-up heating power, 4.3 kW of heating during the 5-second plasma discharge, and then allowed to cool down naturally after the discharge until the cycle is repeated to perform a plasma discharge every 15 min. A small adjustment in the ramp-up timing is required after the first plasma discharge to account for the transient state of the system between subsequent discharges. Ideally there would be zero grams of lithium used during the ramp-up and cool-down phases, and no more than 5.78 g used during the plasma discharge in the conservative case with zero lithium recycling from the plasma. In this simulated scenario, the amount of lithium used in each phase is about 3.11 g during ramp-up, 5.74 g during the plasma discharge (assuming zero lithium recycling), and 22.92 g during the cool-down, making the cool-down the part of the cycle responsible for the largest portion of the lithium evaporation. It is worth noting that tokamak operation at the highest performance may require longer periods between plasma discharges, in which case the 30 W level of evaporator pre-heating can be used to prevent re-solidification of the lithium during these longer intervals without a significant change to the total amount of lithium used, as discussed in Sect. 4. In a power plant, the evaporator system would not be cycled as often as is required for experiments in a shortpulse tokamak. However, for near-term testing of the lithium vapor divertor concept this additional lithium evaporation

will need to be managed carefully. Depending on the allowed lithium inventories in experimental devices, it may be preferable to add active cooling to the system to bring the temperature down more quickly after a plasma discharge and reduce the amount of lithium that is evaporated during the cool-down. As discussed before, any reduction in the thermal mass of the system, particularly the lithium CPS, will improve the thermal responsiveness of the system and thereby reduce the amount of lithium evaporation between discharges. Ultimately the thickness of the components will be constrained by the available fabrication methods as well as considerations for the mechanical reliability of the system in a tokamak environment. These points will be addressed in future work.

## Conclusions and Future Work

In this work, general design considerations for a lithium vapor divertor system are discussed in the context of experiments in a short-pulse tokamak. The transient power balance of the system poses a significant challenge, both in terms of achieving controllability of the lithium evaporation rate and minimizing the amount of lithium that is evaporated in between plasma discharges. An updated design is proposed where the lithium evaporator is moved out of the line-ofsight of the plasma, eliminating the plasma radiation as an input factor in the control of the system during plasma discharges. With a rough design for the geometry of the divertor module, a simplified geometric model with material-dependent parameters is introduced for modeling the thermal cycling of the embedded heater and lithium capillary porous system (CPS). By maintaining the system temperature above about 300 C, the range of thermal cycling can be reduced to minimize stresses on the system while minimizing unnecessary evaporation of lithium between discharges. A strategy for cyclical operation of the system is developed to minimize the amount of lithium evaporated between discharges while maintaining a nearly constant rate of evaporation during the plasma discharge period. This involves ramping up the temperature immediately before the plasma discharge at the fastest rate possible, dropping the power to the level required for the plasma discharge phase just before the plasma is initiated and allowing the thermal inertia of the system to bring it to its final operating temperature, and allowing the evaporative cooling of the system to cool down the system immediately after the discharge. While the quantitative details of this work are unique to the predicted conditions of high-powered operation in the NSTX-U tokamak, the approach can easily be applied to variations of the geometric design, choice of materials, or expected divertor conditions as relevant to the implementation of a lithium evaporator in any tokamak.

Several challenges remain to be addressed with the design that is discussed here. With no direct line-of-sight from the lithium CPS to the divertor plasma, the walls of the evaporator module will need to be hot enough to reflect lithium so that it reaches the plasma, and so that recycled lithium from the plasma does not accumulate on the walls of the box. Radiative heating by the plasma deposited on the upper section of the module will help to accomplish this, but additional heating power or insulation of the exterior of the upper section of the module may be required. Toward this end, ongoing SOLPS-ITER simulations will identify self-consistent operating points under a variety of lithium reflection conditions with this divertor module geometry. With regard to the temperature control, the fast time response and accuracy of radiated power measurements could be suitable for feedback control of the heaters and should be investigated in future work. Despite the remaining challenges, key issues impacting the controllability of a lithium vapor divertor in a short-pulse tokamak have been addressed in this work. There is now ongoing work to prototype individual components needed for laboratory testing of a full-scale divertor module, including 3D printing of the capillary porous structure and the entire module enclosure.
